extracted.intended_audience: general readers, sports journalists, and policy watchers interested in Tokyo 2020 / Olympic governance controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, rules, and expectations governing behaviour, safety, broadcasting, media, and logistics related to the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, as reported in a Wikipedia article on controversies. Covers athlete conduct rules, worker-safety metrics, broadcasting and media norms, and diplomatic sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of political gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC published guidelines prohibiting athletes from using political gestures, such as kneeling, hand gestures, and disrespect during medal ceremonies. Athletes were allowed to express political views on traditional and social media, and in interviews outside the Olympic Village.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the IOC launched a probe into Raven Saunders' podium X-gesture to see if it violated rules prohibiting demonstrations; the USOC defended it as a peaceful expression. The IOC applies these prohibitions when assessing athlete actions at Olympic venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olympic Charter Article 50 — ban on demonstrations/propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 50 of the Olympic Charter prohibits 'any kind of demonstration or political, religious and racial propaganda in Olympic venues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IOC investigates incidents under Article 50 (e.g., Chinese cyclists wearing Mao Zedong pin badges were subject to investigation). The IOC states stadiums should be free of political demonstration and decides on issues case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC standard for medal table ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC standard ranks NOCs by number of gold medals, then silver, then bronze (not by total medals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some media (notably many American outlets) rank by total medals, which has historically produced public controversy; switching between methods can be perceived as biased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on criticizing rival Olympic bids
rubrics_metrics.description: IOC rules prohibit bid proponents and officials from publicly criticising rival bids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Naoki Inose's critical remarks about rival bids were viewed as violating IOC rules and drew international criticism; such statements can lead to reputational consequences and calls for apology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting standards — avoid stereotypes and insensitive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters and official coverage should avoid insensitive, stereotypical, or offensive representations of countries and peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: South Korean broadcaster MBC used insensitive country profiles during the parade of nations and issued an apology. Broadcasters are expected to represent nations respectfully and correct mistakes publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media accuracy and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and media outlets must verify information before reporting and correct errors transparently when they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Indian news outlet ANI wrongly reported an ITA doping test for a weightlifter; WADA and ITA debunked the claim and ANI later called it an 'inadvertent error'. Erroneous reports that remain online can perpetuate misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker overtime and overwork thresholds as safety criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive overtime at construction sites and related workplaces is a measurable safety/labour concern (examples cited: 211 hours 56 minutes overtime in one month; inspectors found employees working more than 80 hours/month overtime; some exceeded 150 hours/month).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numeric overtime figures were linked to suicide and condemned by labour organizations; reports also documented 'dangerous patterns of overwork' such as working up to 28 consecutive days. Such metrics are used by inspectors to identify illegal/unsafe labour practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer obligations on worker safety and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers/contractors are expected to provide safe working conditions, allow reporting of poor conditions, and supply necessary protective equipment rather than forcing workers to purchase it or discouraging complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reports that construction workers (many migrant) were discouraged from reporting poor conditions or required to buy PPE; Mitsubishi Electric case where workers were locked out, forced to attend humiliating training, and publicly apologise. Trade unions and global unions condemned harassment and filed complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vetting of ceremony officials and cultural-sensitivity screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Organising committees should screen creative directors, producers, and ceremony personnel for past discriminatory, offensive, or abusive remarks/behaviour; failure to vet can lead to public backlash and resignations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Yoshiro Mori resigned after sexist remarks; Kentarō Kobayashi was dismissed after past Holocaust jokes; Keigo Oyamada resigned over past bullying allegations. Public and media scrutiny can force staffing changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag and symbol policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of politically or historically sensitive flags and symbols (e.g., Rising Sun Flag, political badges) at Olympic venues may be restricted or banned because they can be seen as offensive or political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: South Korea called for a ban on the Rising Sun Flag; FIFA bans the flag in its competitions. The IOC responds to flag/symbol issues on a case-by-case basis and enforces the Olympic Charter's prohibition on political demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Athlete attire and emblem compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Team uniforms and athlete apparel must comply with hosting-region regulations and governing-body rules; official emblems may require prior approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hong Kong badminton player Ng Ka Long's replacement shirt lacked the correct bauhinia emblem; regional regulations require emblem approval by the chief executive. Sponsors and associations may need to issue corrected jerseys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary and enforcement mechanisms for misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Organising bodies and federations have the authority to disqualify, eject, suspend, or dismiss coaches, officials, and athletes for abusive, racist, or otherwise prohibited conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: German modern pentathlon coach Kim Raisner was disqualified for hitting a horse; Belarusian coaches were ejected after the Tsimanouskaya incident; German cycling director Patrick Moster was fired for a racist slur. Enforcement actions are used to uphold conduct standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and host responsibility to moderate online abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media platforms and host nations/media are expected to take action against online abuse of athletes by removing hate content and sanctioning abusive accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: After sustained online abuse of shooter Wang Luyao, Weibo temporarily banned 33 accounts and deleted hate comments. Platforms may also see counter-campaigns defending athletes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical transparency and fairness of timing/scoring systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical systems (timing, sensors, judging/scoring) must be reliable, transparent, and open to scrutiny when results are contested (ties, judging disputes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Four swimming heats recorded tied results and raised questions about pool sensor timing; FINA stated there was 'nothing wrong'. In rhythmic gymnastics, score inquiries can be submitted but may not change outcomes; federations may publish scoring details to clarify decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic sensitivity in naming and cartographic depictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Official materials (maps, team names) should respect international sensitivities and established naming conventions (e.g., 'Chinese Taipei' vs 'Taiwan'); depiction of disputed territories can provoke diplomatic complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Torch-relay map showing Liancourt Rocks and Kuril Islands as part of Japan drew objections from South Korea and Russia; Taiwanese team being introduced as 'Taiwan' drew criticism from Chinese diplomats. Organisers and broadcasters are expected to follow agreed conventions to avoid politicisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on mobilising students for Olympic attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that treat students who do not attend allocated Olympic/Paralympic tickets for schools as absent were criticised as compelling attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism was directed at policies expecting students to attend when schools accepted tickets; however, COVID-19 restrictions ultimately led to many spectators being disallowed from events.
